newsitem.title: UK: IRA says its sniper killed British soldier.
newsitem.headline: IRA says its sniper killed British soldier.

text.p: IRA guerrillas said on Thursday one of its snipers fired the bullet that killed a British soldier two weeks ago and marked an escalation of its campaign against British rule over Northern Ireland.

The Irish Republican Army said in a statement that members of its hardline "South Armagh Brigade" killed Stephen Restorick, 23, as he spoke to a motorist at a checkpoint near a heavily fortified military helicopter base at Bessbrook, near the Irish border.

The statement in An Phoblacht, the weekly paper of Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, came as IRA units in Belfast said they had tried but failed to mount another attack on security forces in the Irish nationalist west of the city.
The IRA statement in the newspaper said its "volunteers" carried out an attack on British forces guarding the Bessbrook helicopter base on February 12.
"One of the soldiers on duty was hit by a single shot and died." Restorick was the second soldier to be killed by the republican extremists in the province since October.
A woman civilian who was speaking to him when he was struck narrowly escaped serious injury. Her head was grazed.
The killing sparked outrage in London, Dublin and Washington and led to further demands that the IRA should abandon its war unconditionally.

IRA violence in recent months has provoked three attacks on Catholic nationalists by banned pro-British Loyalist militants. British security sources say a Loyalist truce remains in force but is shaky.
Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, wants an immediate seat at all-party talks on the future of the province.

A suspected IRA bomb was found near a police base in the heart of Irish nationalist west Belfast on Thursday but a second guerrilla alert in the city seemed to have been a hoax, British security sources said.
Streets around the heavily defended Andersonstown police station were cordoned off while army bomb disposal experts moved in.
"They have found something which is now being looked at," a police source.
Ian Williamson, police commander in west Belfast, condemned the guerrillas for what he termed their "grubby, pathetic but lethal little war".

Police and soldiers launched a separate operation in the Antrim Road area of north Belfast after an IRA message to local media that their "volunteers" had been forced to abandon a powerful mortar bomb in a car after spotting police patrols. Later police said they had checked a suspect car but there was no bomb in it.
